concepts.title: Neuron Structure and Resting Membrane Potential
concepts.section: 18.1 Neural System, 18.2 Human Neural System, 18.3.1 Generation and Conduction of Nerve Impulse
concepts.definition: A neuron has a cell body with cytoplasm and nucleus, dendrites carrying impulses toward the cell, and a long axon ending in synaptic knobs; the resting nerve membrane maintains a resting potential through the sodium potassium pump, keeping the outside positive and the inside negative.
concepts.key_idea: The polarised resting membrane is maintained by active transport of three sodium ions out for two potassium ions in, making the axonal membrane more permeable to potassium ions at rest.
question_patterns: describe the structure of a neuron with its parts

solution_steps.explain: Mark cell body, dendrites, axon and synaptic terminals.
Recall sodium and potassium gradients across the resting membrane.
State that the outside stays positive relative to the inside at rest.

concepts.title: Action Potential Generation and Its Voltage Change
concepts.section: 18.3.1 Generation and Conduction of Nerve Impulse
concepts.definition: When a stimulus depolarises the membrane beyond threshold, sodium channels open and the membrane potential reverses to the peak of the action potential or nerve impulse; the change in voltage equals the peak action potential minus the resting potential, and conduction proceeds as depolarisation spreads along the axon with repolarisation following behind.
concepts.key_idea: The impulse is an all or none self-propagating reversal of membrane polarity, and repolarisation restores the resting state as potassium ions flow outward.
question_patterns: explain how an action potential is generated in a nerve fibre
calculate the voltage change during a nerve impulse from the two potentials
what is depolarisation and repolarisation of the membrane
why is the nerve impulse called all or none
how does the impulse travel along an unmyelinated axon
what is saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres

solution_steps.explain: Deduct the resting potential from the peak action potential to get the voltage swing of the impulse

concepts.title: Synapse and Synaptic Transmission
concepts.definition: At a synapse the axon terminal of one neuron meets the dendrite of another across a synaptic cleft; in chemical synapses calcium entry releases neurotransmitters like acetylcholine from synaptic vesicles that bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, while electrical synapses pass current directly at gap junctions.
concepts.key_idea: Chemical synapses are far more common, and neurotransmitter binding generates a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron, allowing one-way conduction across the cleft.
question_patterns: differentiate chemical and electrical synapses

solution_steps.explain: Check whether transmission is chemical or electrical.
Follow calcium entry, vesicle fusion and transmitter release.
State the new potential generated in the post-synaptic cell.

concepts.title: Human Brain, Reflex Action and Reflex Arc
concepts.section: 18.4 Central Neural System, 18.5 Reflex Action and Reflex Arc
concepts.definition: The human brain divides into forebrain with cerebrum and limbic structures, midbrain and hindbrain with pons, cerebellum and medulla controlling involuntary functions; a reflex action such as the knee jerk travels through a reflex arc of receptor, sensory neuron, CNS centre, motor neuron and effector muscle, with the spinal cord as its centre.
concepts.key_idea: The medulla controls vital involuntary functions like breathing and heart rate, while the cerebellum keeps posture and balance, and reflex arcs protect the body before conscious processing.
question_patterns: describe the parts of the human brain and their functions
define reflex action and draw the reflex arc

differentiate the forebrain midbrain and hindbrain
why is the spinal cord the centre of simple reflexes

solution_steps.explain: Assign forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain their structures.
Link memory, balance, breathing and vision centres to their parts.
Follow receptor to effector through the spinal centre.
